extracted.intended_audience: public relations counselors, corporate communicators, and business executives responsible for PR
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on planning and executing public-relations/propaganda campaigns for businesses: how to study publics, use group psychology and leaders, design campaigns (continuous interpretation vs high-spotting), and align corporate actions with public expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand group structure and mass psychology (not mechanistic individual reaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The new salesmanship understands the group structure of society and the principles of mass psychology rather than treating the mind as an isolated reaction machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than addressing individuals as isolated automatons (reiterating stimulus to form habit), study who influences group behaviour and work through group relations. Example: instead of blanket 'Eat more bacon' ads, persuade physicians to recommend bacon because many people follow doctors' advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and use opinion leaders/influencers
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine 'who is it that influences' the habits of the public and enlist those leaders to project desired ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite or persuade key people (physicians, famous musicians, society leaders, influential architects, judges, art authorities) to endorse or dramatize the idea so that their example propagates through imitation and is then projected to the wider public through publicity channels. Examples: physicians for food habits; violinist and society leader for music-room acceptance; architects making music rooms part of plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create associative/emotional currents through staged circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of direct attack on sales resistance, create circumstances that will swing emotional currents and make for purchaser demand by associating the product with desirable social meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize exhibitions, ceremonies, and events that dramatize an idea (e.g., period music-room exhibits with rare tapestries and staged ceremonies) so the public adopts the idea as its own. Use dramatization to lift an idea into public consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use competitions and group activities to mobilize motives and goodwill
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilize nationwide or local competitions and school/institutional programs to engage groups and psychological motives, thereby turning product use into a personal and collective interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ivory soap sculpture contests run under reputable art institutions and school systems—stimulate esthetic, competitive, gregarious, snobbish, exhibitionist, maternal motives; local contests feed national entries, create practice/use in homes, and build goodwill and acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find disinterested points of coincidence between client and other groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Discover where a client's interests coincide with those of other individuals or groups and emphasize that common ground so leaders will lend authority to the campaign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders will help only if the campaign touches their genuine interests. Examples: soap sculpture promoted by artists/educators for esthetic education; railway helping towns develop industry to mutually benefit; bank offering investment services to help customers and secure deposits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work indirectly by influencing intermediaries and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct campaigns at intermediaries or institutions whose actions affect consumer behaviour rather than always addressing consumers directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: To boost luggage sales, run a campaign aimed at railroads, steamship companies, baggage handlers, and foreign governments to change baggage handling and costs; these institutional changes will increase luggage demand. Similarly, have hospitals and school systems test gelatine (scientific endorsement) before projecting results to leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scientific validation and respected institutional endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ research findings and reputable institutional testing to validate product claims and then use leaders and institutions to spread the validated idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mellon Institute research on gelatine’s nutritive benefits used in hospitals and schools; favorable test results projected to other leaders to create momentum. Contests held under reputable art galleries or institutions lend prestige to promotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between continuous interpretation and high-spotting
rubrics_metrics.description: PR work generally reduces to two types: continuous interpretation (control every approach so the public receives the desired impression often unconsciously) and dramatization by high-spotting (vivid events/acts that seize attention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which method (or combination) fits objectives after a full study. Example of high-spotting: making a building ten feet taller than others as dramatization. Continuous interpretation is persistent, subtle shaping of impression across every contact point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize and control every public contact to express corporate personality
rubrics_metrics.description: At every point where a business touches the public, express its personality and objectives in terms the public can understand—architecture, product presentation, delivery, officers’ conduct, cleanliness, available services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: bakery using hygienic wrapping and clean delivery wagons; store architecture conveying authenticity; a bank opening a prestigious branch to project appeal. Even trivial details (doorman politeness, clerk dress) matter in conveying the intended image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be truthful and avoid false pretenses or exaggerated claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations must not be mere protective coloring to hide real aims; false impressions and exaggerated claims are bad business and immoral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sound PR policy interprets the business 'vividly and truly' through every avenue; do not feature a few high-class items to mislead about the main stock. Maintain honesty to preserve long-term goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study and adapt to public standards, prejudices, and habits; do not run counter to them
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn the public's standards and operate within them—modify them gradually by working through leaders rather than attempting to 'mold' an amorphous mass at will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You cannot compel a whole generation to accept sudden changes (e.g., fashion), but can persuade via leaders to adopt variations (example: evening dresses long in back). Respect public personalities and work to bring business and public into friendly agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to responsibilities toward multiple stakeholder groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize responsibilities to stockholders, dealers, industry peers, retailers, consumers, and the broader public; each has legitimate informational and ethical expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide stockholders with information and appeals to use the product; invite dealers to factories; refrain from unfair selling claims that harm the industry; keep factories clean and open to inspection to satisfy consumers. Neglect of any stakeholder can harm public goodwill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change the business itself if necessary to align with public demand
rubrics_metrics.description: PR counsel may recommend modifications ranging from broad policy shifts to trivial execution details when these changes better align the business with public objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: transforming product lines; featuring medium-priced goods to attract future high-end customers; hiring college grads as clerks; engaging artists for window design; canceling branches if reputational scandal occurs. PR is not only messaging but also recommending operational changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage psychological motives and gratification to mobilize supporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Design campaigns that tap familiar motives (esthetic, competitive, gregarious, snobbish, exhibitionist, maternal) so people will work for the client's cause for intrinsic gratification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: soap-sculpture contests set multiple motives in motion and created mass practice/use because participants found the activity itself gratifying; leaders and group formations channel these motives into support for the client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and maintain public goodwill continuously because opinion can reverse
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if public opinion presently favors big business or certain industries, it can change; PR must be watchful and maintain contact at all corporate touchpoints to prevent backlash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: critiques exposing misleading financial statements or non-voting shares can erode confidence; utilities are especially vulnerable to demands for public ownership. Continuous care and transparency are required to preserve goodwill.
